source_read: PDF, pp. 31-36 (all pages; commentary without tables or figures).

claims.note: The complacency and positive-seeking points are the authors' arguments without data, as the claim says, and the conclusion does support distributing strips with guidance on reading results and low-threshold naloxone. Two qualifications for the editor: (1) the only behavioural figures McGowan relays (a health authority's release: clients who tested before use and got a positive result 10 times more likely to reduce their dose, and those who reduced 25% less likely to overdose; FORECAST: 70% of 256 said knowing about fentanyl would change their behaviour) are second-hand, from a small self-selected minority or stated intentions, and are not a comparison of people given or not given strips, so they do not contradict the claim; (2) McGowan relays the manufacturer and an unpublished DanceSafe/UCSF evaluation saying the strips detected carfentanil, even at very low concentrations, which runs against the claim's relay (from the scoping review) of strips missing carfentanil; the claim could note that this is disputed.

anchors.locator: Testing for fentanyl and fentanyl analogues, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Insite evaluation: 86% of all samples and 90% of heroin samples tested positive for fentanyl, probably an overestimate (62% of checks after use; people test drugs they suspect). The authors argue that frequent positive results, especially after use without ill effects, can lead to complacency and limit risk-reduction measures; no data are given.

anchors.locator: Testing for fentanyl and fentanyl analogues, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Health Canada warned that off-label consumer use could give false negatives; the authors add that false positives, or positives below psychoactive levels, may also do harm.

anchors.locator: What do we need to know about fentanyl self-testing? > Effect, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Because some people who use drugs want fentanyl, a positive result may be sought after, or at least not deter use, particularly during withdrawal; argued, not measured.

anchors.locator: What do we need to know about fentanyl self-testing? > Effect, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Strips give no indication of how much fentanyl or analogue is present; the authors say it is unclear whether routine positives at non-fatal concentrations, or for less potent analogues, will promote complacency.

The authors favour distributing strips with clear guidance on interpreting results, alongside low-threshold naloxone and broader harm reduction, and encouraging use only with someone who has naloxone, to mitigate false negatives and complacency.

anchors.locator: What do we need to know about fentanyl self-testing? > Acceptability, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Insite averaged 4.7 checks a day among about 600 daily users; a health-authority release (positive result before use: 10 times more likely to reduce the dose; dose reducers 25% less likely to overdose) refers to that small minority; FORECAST: 73% of 256 were interested in knowing whether fentanyl was present and 70% said knowing would make them change their behaviour.

anchors.locator: Testing for fentanyl and fentanyl analogues, 3rd paragraph
anchors.extracted: The manufacturer says the strips detect carfentanil and other analogues; an unpublished DanceSafe/UCSF evaluation reported that they detected most analogues, including carfentanil at very low concentrations (both second-hand).

claims.note: 'Relays a preliminary study in which 7 of 70 samples gave erroneous or invalid results' is exact (7/70 = 10.0%, Wilson 4.9-19.2, editors' calculation). The study is unnamed and cited through Health Canada and a news story; McGowan does not say who ran the tests (staff or people who use drugs) or what counted as erroneous, so it is not evidence about home use specifically. McGowan also relays a laboratory-versus-user contrast for another device (Quest & Horsley, 2007: a date-rape drug drink test 100% accurate in the laboratory but 65% in users' hands, sensitivity 50%, specificity 91.6%), the only quantified lab-versus-user comparison in these five sources; the claim could cite it beside Murray, labelled second-hand and indirect.

anchors.locator: Testing for fentanyl and fentanyl analogues, 3rd paragraph (begins p. 32)
anchors.extracted: A preliminary study of strip efficacy found 7 of 70 drug samples gave erroneous or invalid results, after which Health Canada limited its endorsement to supervised consumption sites (cited via Health Canada and a CBC news story). Same paragraph: the maker reports over 98% accuracy in urine; preliminary FORECAST data gave the strips the lowest detection limit and the highest sensitivity (96% and 100% at two sites) and specificity (90% and 98%) of the three technologies compared.

anchors.locator: Self-testing of club drugs using reagent kits, 1st-2nd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Relays Murray et al. (reduced sensitivity and specificity, considerable scope for misreading by people unfamiliar with the reagents; the same study the claim cites) and Quest & Horsley (2007): a drink test for GHB and ketamine was 100% accurate in the laboratory but 65% when used by users (sensitivity 50%, specificity 91.6%).

anchors.locator: Testing for fentanyl and fentanyl analogues, 4th paragraph
anchors.extracted: Unclear whether sensitivity and specificity differ with how strips are used in practice; the effect of acidifiers is unknown; the dissolving solution has reduced the accuracy of reagent tests; the 2-5 minutes needed to read a result may be impractical when injecting on the street.

key_findings.correction: Confirmed for what McGowan prints (0.13 mg/ml; 96% and 100%; 90% and 98%); the editors' comparison with Green et al. (2020) was not checked here (not among my sources).
The 63/70 = 90% inference is plausible; McGowan gives no source for the 90%.

reporting_issues.note: Confirmed that 0.13 mg/ml is printed; the comparison with the Green et al. card was not checked here.
